text: Coordinated enemy behavior in an Unreal Engine 5.7 action-puzzle platformer

Introduce the AI as one part of RGB's main gameplay loop. The system coordinates several enemies while allowing each enemy type to retain its own movement and attack behavior. The presentation focuses on the design problem, the architecture, the three enemy variants, and the technical choices behind the implementation.

Source: ENEMY_AI_SYSTEM_EXPLAINED.txt, document summary and section 14.
Several enemies should create pressure without creating chaos
Enemies need distinct movement and attack identities
Only a limited number should attack simultaneously
Telegraphs must give the player time to react
Designers need behavior they can tune and debug

Begin with the player experience. If every enemy independently runs straight at the player and attacks as soon as possible, encounters become crowded and difficult to read. RGB therefore needs both variety and control: enemies should feel active, but their attacks should remain understandable and fair.

Source: ENEMY_AI_SYSTEM_EXPLAINED.txt, overview and section 4.
Arena control owns activation, respawn, reset, and completion
C++ owns gameplay rules. Blueprints provide assets and tuning.

The coordinator makes decisions that require shared knowledge, such as choosing attackers or reserving a teleport destination. Each enemy actor then executes its own movement and attack. Arena control sits around both layers and handles lifecycle events. This structure avoids one enormous AI class while still giving the group consistent rules.

Source: ENEMY_AI_SYSTEM_EXPLAINED.txt, sections 1 and 4.
Action states make behavior visible and debuggable
Roles describe each enemy’s current job
Occupies a side of the player
Leases expire, and commitment time reduces rapid role swapping

The shared action-state enum gives all enemy variants the same language for debugging. Coordination roles answer a different question: what job should this enemy perform for the group? Assignments have a lease, so an enemy cannot follow stale instructions forever. Commitment time also prevents two similarly positioned enemies from repeatedly swapping roles.

Source: ENEMY_AI_SYSTEM_EXPLAINED.txt, sections 2, 3, and 4.
The group coordinates scarce opportunities while each actor executes locally

The coordinator updates on a timer. It removes invalid references, finds the player, gathers candidates, sorts them, and preserves an existing committed attacker when appropriate. It then selects up to the configured maximum. Attack permission and teleport reservations operate like shared resources that enemies must acquire before continuing.

Source: ENEMY_AI_SYSTEM_EXPLAINED.txt, section 4.
Damage happens only after the windup and a fresh range check
This keeps the attack readable and prevents stale hits

The ground enemy patrols only when no coordinated movement takes priority. A forward sphere sweep detects blocking geometry, while a downward trace checks for safe ground ahead. Detection uses a larger lose-interest range to prevent rapid target flickering. During an attack, a delayed timer performs a fresh range check before applying damage.

Source: ENEMY_AI_SYSTEM_EXPLAINED.txt, sections 5 and 6.
Discover tagged Target Points once at startup
Reject occupied, repeated, reserved, or nearby points
Blend player proximity with a random score
Reserve during the visible charge and validate again
Use a warned area attack when the player remains close
Closer points are favored, but the result remains unpredictable

Level designers place and tag the legal teleport points. The enemy filters unsafe choices, scores the remaining points using randomness and player proximity, and reserves the winner before charging. At the end of the charge, it validates the capsule location again. Its area attack follows the same fairness rule: warn first, then recheck the player before damage.

Source: ENEMY_AI_SYSTEM_EXPLAINED.txt, section 8.
Move toward the live player position
Acceleration, swept collision, sliding, camera-zone clamp
Local steering handles nearby geometry without a full path planner

The flyer calculates a desired velocity from pursuit, separation, and obstacle avoidance. It approaches that velocity gradually, which produces smoother motion. Movement uses collision sweeps and a second slide movement after a hit. Before moving, the target position is clamped to the camera zone so the enemy stays within the active arena.

Source: ENEMY_AI_SYSTEM_EXPLAINED.txt, section 7.
Grounded enemies can transfer their color to the platform beneath them
Arena control records spawn configuration, removes eliminated enemies from coordination, and restores configured instances after the delay

Enemy AI is tied directly to the color puzzle. A hit only succeeds when the projectile color matches the enemy. On elimination, a grounded enemy can transfer its color to its current RGB platform. Arena control then handles event cleanup and optionally restores the same configured enemy instance after a fixed or progress-scaled delay.

Source: ENEMY_AI_SYSTEM_EXPLAINED.txt, sections 9 and 10.
Why deterministic C++ AI was chosen
Unreal-MAP was investigated as a reinforcement-learning option
Automated simulations, learned cooperation, strategy comparison
Python training pipeline, new environment interfaces, extra dependencies, UE 4.27 to 5.7 migration work
Continue with the established state-based C++ architecture

Directly tunable in Unreal
Easier to debug
Achievable within project scope
Reinforcement learning remains a possible future research direction

Unreal-MAP could support training and evaluation across many simulated encounters. However, it is a broader research environment rather than a small AI plugin. Integrating it would require communication interfaces, observations, actions, rewards, episode reset logic, and engine-version migration. Since RGB already had working C++ AI, deterministic coordination offered the best balance of quality and scope.

Source: ENEMY_AI_SYSTEM_EXPLAINED.txt, section 15.
Distinct movement for three enemy types
The current system is a stable, debuggable base for more advanced enemy decision-making

Close by separating completed work from future ideas. The current implementation already coordinates attacks, handles three specialized enemy types, integrates with color combat, and manages arena lifecycle. It does not yet provide global navigation, puzzle-aware sabotage, cannon tactics, or networking. Those limitations define a clear direction for future work rather than weakening the current system.

Source: ENEMY_AI_SYSTEM_EXPLAINED.txt, sections 12, 13, and 16.
